paper_title: LEV: Thinking Fast and Deep with Looped Decision Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Decision models answer typed questions about an input with one probability per option, computed in a single forward pass without generating text. Like the fast System 1 of dual-process theory, they answer at once, but their depth is fixed at training time, so they spend the same computation on easy and hard questions. Models that reason in generated text can think longer, but they pay for every extra step in decoded tokens. We present LEV, a decision model that thinks deeper by rerunning its layers in a loop instead of generating tokens. LEV builds on a language model pretrained as a loop, reads the options after every loop step and trains all steps jointly, so one checkpoint can answer at any depth. On three looped backbones, accuracy rises with depth on the same weights, mostly on hard questions, and a 2.6B LEV goes from 63.2% at depth one to 76.2% at depth four on JevBench. On-demand depth, set per question by a small stopper with a threshold fitted on unlabelled requests, saves 15% to 24% of the computation at a cost of under one accuracy point, level with or slightly above a fixed mix of depths. On a locked test set, the 1.4B and 3B models are 5.4 to 8.8 points more accurate than dense (non-looped) models and cascades of the same latency below 50 ms.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Generative language models that reason with chain-of-thought act as System 2 (Kahneman, 2011). They write out their reasoning before choosing an option, so every decision is slow, even an easy one (Villalón, 2026; razorback16, 2026), and turning the reasoning off lowers their accuracy markedly on JevBench (Standhartinger, 2026). Decision models such as Jev (TypeSafe AI, 2026) and Kev (Palmer, 2026) are System 1 for questions with fixed set of options. They return probability for each option from one forward pass (Devlin et al., 2019; Robinson et al., 2023) in tens of milliseconds, but they spend the same computation on every question and cannot think longer on hard one. Not every question needs more computation. On the public JevBench items, Kev-4B answers 28 more items correctly than Kev-0.8B, and Figure 2a shows that all of them come from the standard and hard tiers, because both models already answer every easy item. decision model that could add computation only where it pays off would keep the speed of the small model on easy questions and approach the accuracy of the large one on hard questions. Existing ways to spend more computation without generating text fall short for decision models (Section 3). cascade passes uncertain questions to larger model (Varshney & 1 Figure 1 (a) Loop steps that on-demand LEV-2.6B spends per JevBench tier. (b) LevBench test accuracy against latency, with the Pareto frontiers of LEV over all depths (solid) and of dense models and cascades (dashed). Arrows mark the gap of ondemand LEV-3B to the dense frontier. (c) JevBench accuracy of LEV-2.6B on the standard and hard tiers at depth one, on demand, and at depth four, against the dense Qwen3.5-4B control. Baral, 2022; Chen et al., 2024), but reads them again and needs second model. Early exit stops at confident intermediate layer (Xin et al., 2020; Schuster et al., 2022; Elhoushi et al., 2024), but these layers are not trained to be read and are often confidently wrong on new data (Meronen et al., 2024). loop reruns the same layers without adding parameters (Dehghani et al., 2019; Geiping et al., 2025), but added to pretrained model it barely helps, as Jev-LCT (Cao, 2026) reports, unless it gets far more continued pretraining than decision model is trained on (McLeish et al., 2025; Koishekenov et al., 2025). We propose LEV, System 1.5 decision model (Wang et al., 2025) that thinks in loops rather than tokens. LEV builds on natively looped language models (Zhu et al., 2025; Nanbeige Lab, 2026), whose loop is trained in pretraining rather than added afterwards. Decision training therefore does not have to teach the model to use its loop, whereas loop added to pretrained decision model stays unused (Section 3). shared readout scores the options after each step and all steps are trained jointly, so one set of weights answers at any depth, and further step resumes from the previous hidden states without reading the input again. lightweight stopper sets the depth of each question on demand by predicting whether its answer already agrees with the deepest one, with threshold set on unlabelled requests. We use this target because the usual early-exit rule, confidence threshold set on labelled data, does not beat fixed mix of depths here, as shallow readouts are overconfident on new data. Since the target is the models own deepest answer, deployment can fit the stopper on its own traffic without labels. We build LEV on three looped backbones and evaluate it on JevBench and two held-out benchmarks. Accuracy rises with depth on the same weights, mostly on hard questions (Figure 1c), and the stopper spends more steps on harder questions without seeing their difficulty (Figure 1a). On-demand depth saves 15% to 24% of the computation at cost of under one accuracy point, level with or slightly above fixed mix of depths. locked test, read once after the recipe and the stopper were fixed, confirms that on-demand depth stays within one point of the deepest readout. Below 50 ms, the 1.4B and 3B models are 5.4 to 8.8 points more accurate than dense (non-looped) models and cascades of the same latency (Figure 1b). Our contributions are as follows. We propose LEV, System 1.5 decision model that thinks deeper on hard questions through loop steps rather than generated text. It reads the options after every step of natively looped backbone, so one checkpoint serves every depth. We show that stopper whose threshold is set on unlabelled requests gives on-demand depth without labels. It predicts agreement with the deepest answer rather than correctness, and it is level with or above fixed mix of depths where confidence thresholds set on labelled data fall below it. On three looped backbones, LEV gains most from depth on hard questions, and below 50 ms it is more accurate than dense models and cascades of the same latency. We also build LevBench, benchmark frozen before any model read it, whose tiers move step by step away from the training data.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Decision models. Decision models score options discriminatively in one forward pass (Devlin et al., 2019; Zaratiana et al., 2024; Robinson et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024), and block attention masks let independent questions share that pass (Ratner et al., 2023). Jev and its open reimplementation Kev read the options with pointer head (Vinyals et al., 2015). generative model can also answer such questions by naming an option, but it must bind each option to its symbol (Robinson et al., 2023) and is sensitive to the order and labels of the options (Zheng et al., 2024). Open Jev-style servers such as djev (Villalón, 2026) and OpenJev (razorback16, 2026) follow this generative route and can add reasoning text before the answer, which raises accuracy on hard questions at the price of decoding time on every question. decision model instead scores the options themselves in one pass, and its probabilities can be calibrated with single temperature (Guo et al., 2017). LEV adds per-question depth to such model through backbone pretrained as loop. Looped models and adaptive computation. Looped transformers rerun one block of layers to add computation without adding parameters (Dehghani et al., 2019; Giannou et al., 2023), and looped language models such as Ouro (Zhu et al., 2025) reason better with more iterations and can be read at several depths 2 Figure 2 Evidence for depth chosen per question. (a) Outcome of each public JevBench item under Kev-0.8B and Kev-4B. (b) Gain over Kev-0.8B when Kev-4B answers random half, the least confident half, or all items. (c) Single read against generated reasoning on the same base model, with latencies from published results on different endpoints. (d) Accuracy change from loops retrofitted onto Qwen3.5-0.8B, each row changing one setting of the default. (Geiping et al., 2025; Saunshi et al., 2025; Jeddi et al., 2026; Popescu et al., 2026). loop added to standard pretrained model needs adapters or continued pretraining (Bae et al., 2025; McLeish et al., 2025) and otherwise tends to stay unused (Chen et al., 2026; Shapiro, 2026). Adaptive computation stops early through halting (Graves, 2016) or confident exits (Xin et al., 2020; Elbayad et al., 2020; Schwartz et al., 2020), or adds latent tokens (Hao et al., 2025; Goyal et al., 2024), and its shallow exits are often overconfident (Meronen et al., 2024) unless calibrated toward the full model, as in CALM (Schuster et al., 2022). CATs (Schuster et al., 2021) likewise predicts whether an exit agrees with the full model, and BERxiT (Xin et al., 2021) learns when to exit from labelled data. LEV instead trains every loop step as decision model, stops whole steps without adding positions, and sets the threshold of its stopper on unlabelled requests.

sections.title: 3 Motivation
sections.content: A decision model spends the same computation on every question. To test whether this is good use of computation, we compare the released Kev-0.8B and Kev-4B, trained on the same sources, item by item on the 231 public JevBench items (Section A), and we try three ways of adding computation. They lead to two observations. Observation 1: Extra computation pays off on few questions, and cheap first read finds them. (1) The gain comes from hard questions. Kev-4B answers 28 more items correctly than Kev-0.8B, and Figure 2a shows that this gain comes entirely from the standard and hard tiers, because both models already answer every easy item. (2) The small model can tell which questions need more. The two models reach different outcomes on only 42 of the 231 items, yet Kev-4B spends its extra parameters on every item. The confidence of Kev-0.8B finds these items. As Figure 2b shows, sending its least confident half to Kev-4B nearly matches Kev-4B on all items. (1) Cascades Observation 2: Existing ways to add computation cost too much or stay unused. read uncertain questions twice. Kev-0.8B already takes 79 ms at the median against 108 ms for Kev-4B, so every item the cascade of Figure 2b passes on takes longer than Kev-4B alone, is read again from the start, and needs second model to host. (2) Thinking in tokens pays on every question. JevBench scores two open Jev-style servers, djev (Villalón, 2026) and OpenJev (razorback16, 2026), with and without generated reasoning on the same DiffusionGemma 26B base model. These results in Figure 2c show that thinking raises hard accuracy by 9 to 13 points but makes the median hard item three to four times slower, and every question pays for its reasoning text, including easy ones. (3) Retrofitted loops stay closed. We loop eight middle layers of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, the backbone of Kev-0.8B, behind per-channel gates that start at zero, and train the model with Kevs recipe (Section A.3). sections.title: 6 Main Results
sections.content: Table 1 supports four conclusions. (1) Extra loop steps raise accuracy on the same weights, with diminishing returns. The gain holds for every backbone and on every panel and reaches 13.0 points on JevBench for LEV-2.6B (Figure 13), while the fourth step of the Ouro models adds at most one point. Most of the gain comes with the first extra step, which lifts the held-out average of LEV-2.6B from 51.3% to 62.0%, against 65.7% at depth four. It is also smallest on the training sources, as LEV-1.4B and LEV-2.6B gain about 7 points on Kev-Seen from depth one to depth four, against 9.0 to 19.5 points on the four panels further from the training data. (2) One checkpoint covers several operating points and can beat dense control at the same latency. LEV-3B at depth one is 4.0 points above Qwen3-1.7B on the held-out average at 23 against 22 ms, and LEV-2.6B at depth two is 3.1 points above Qwen3.5-2B at 101 against 105 ms, while Qwen3-1.7B is level with or above LEV-1.4B (Figure 4). (3) LEV matches larger models with fewer parameters but not fewer operations. LEV-3B is level with Qwen3.5-4B on JevBench, and LEV-2.6B with the released Kev-4B (Figure 13), but each loop step runs the whole backbone. (4) On-demand depth saves computation at almost no cost in accuracy and beats dense cascades at low latency (Sections 7.2 and 7.4). sections.title: 7 Analysis
sections.content: We analyse LEV through five research questions. RQ1 asks where extra depth helps, by difficulty tier, by revision between steps, and by application area. RQ2 asks whether on-demand depth is more accurate than fixed mix of depths at the same cost, and RQ3 asks which stopping rule makes it so. RQ4 compares LEV with dense models and cascades at the same measured latency, and RQ5 asks how joint training, more data, and full-weight fine-tuning change the accuracy at each depth.

sections.content: The gain over the fixed-depth frontier depends on its shape. Against fixed depth of the same cost, the gain is small. On-demand LEV-2.6B is 1.4 points above the fixed-depth frontier on the tuning panels but only 0.2 points on the held-out panels, while LEV-3B gains 1.0 point there. In Figure 6 the frontier of the Ouro models is concave because the first extra step brings most of the gain, whereas the two-step frontier of LEV-3B is straight line that most stopping signals beat. The locked test confirms the development result. On the test partitions of both held-out panels, read once after the backbones, the recipe, and the stopper were fixed, on-demand depth again loses at most 1.0 point against the deepest readout, is above the frontier for LEV-1.4B and LEV-3B, and is level with it for LEV-2.6B (stars in Figure 6). Harder and less familiar items get more steps. The stopper follows difficulty without seeing it. On JevBench, on-demand LEV-2.6B uses 1.2, 2.4, and 3.0 steps on easy, standard, and hard items (Figure 1a). On LevBench it computes 66% of the deepest pass on the id tier, 1.8 points above the frontier, and 75% to 87% on the tiers further from the training data (Figure 5d), and the same holds on further panels and on harder generated questions (Table 12 and Figure 7). sections.title:
7.3 RQ3: How should the depth be chosen?
Confidence thresholds set on labelled data do not beat the frontier. The usual early-exit rule stops
once the top probability reaches a threshold chosen for accuracy on the labelled calibration partition. For the
Ouro models, Figure 8 shows that neither this rule nor other early-exit rules, thresholds on the margin or
entropy and patience-based exit (Zhou et al., 2020), beat the frontier.
sections.content: Shallow confidence is overconfident and blind to fixable errors. Two properties of the shallow readouts explain this  (Table 14)  . First, they are overconfident on new data. The questions that LEV-2.6B stops at depth one are 94.8% correct on the calibration partition but only 78.9% on Kev-Transfer, at almost the same confidence. Second, confidence separates right from wrong answers with an AUROC of 0.67 to 0.83, but separates the wrong answers that more steps fix from the rest with only 0.46 to 0.61. sections.content: More data mainly strengthens the shallow readouts. All other results use 31,329 training records (Train-31k), which we extend to 60k and 120k (Train-60k and Train-120k, Section B.3). On the pooled held-out panels, depth one of LEV-2.6B rises from 50.5% to 62.9% and the deepest readout from 65.3% to 73.0%, so on-demand cost falls from 0.76 to 0.63 (Figure 11b). Part of this rise is in distribution, because the larger sets add sources that LevBench also draws on. On Kev-Breadth, which no training set touches, 10 the deepest readout stays between 67.3% and 67.7%, while Qwen3.5-2B gains 0.4 points and Qwen3.5-4B 2.0 points  (Table 20)  . LoRA beats full-weight fine-tuning on the Ouro models. Training all weights, shaded in Figure 11b, lowers the deepest readout of both Ouro models by 1.3 to 1.9 points and removes their gain over the frontier, while LEV-3B is unchanged  (Table 19)  . Brier term, step weights that grow with the step, and more loop steps than in pretraining change the deepest readout by at most 0.9 points and raise its gain over the frontier by at most 0.1 points  (Table 22)  . The hard-tier ECE of every readout lies between 0.18 and 0.26 after temperature scaling with no trend in depth, as for the Qwen3-1.7B control, so the gap to Kev and Jev comes from our single-stage recipe rather than from the loop  (Table 9)  .

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: We build LEV, decision model that thinks in loop steps rather than tokens. One checkpoint serves several operating points whose accuracy rises with depth, mostly on hard questions. Setting the stopping threshold on unlabelled requests saves 15% to 24% of the computation at cost of under one accuracy point, and below 50 ms the 1.4B and 3B models are 5.4 to 8.8 points more accurate than dense models and cascades of the same latency. The stopper spends more steps on harder questions without seeing their difficulty, and predicting agreement with the deepest answer works where confidence thresholds set on labelled data do not. These results suggest that natively looped backbone turns depth into setting chosen at serving time, so one decision model can trade latency for accuracy per question instead of per deployment. Two directions follow from the analysis. stopping target that also recovers the questions shallower step answers correctly could add accuracy beyond the deepest readout, and larger looped backbones would show whether the gains on hard questions grow with scale.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Our study covers looped backbones of 1.4B to 3B parameters, the sizes that are publicly available, and applying the same recipe to larger looped models would show how far the depth curve extends. We report JevBench results on its 231 public items, and further decision benchmarks would broaden the picture. We count the cost of on-demand depth in loop steps, and serving path that batches requests at different depths would turn this saving into wall-clock time. Finally, latency is measured one request at time without fused kernels, graph capture or state caching for all systems, and optimised serving for looped and dense models alike is left to future work.

sections.title: E Stopping Rules
sections.content: E.1 Stopper and Top-Probability Rule Stopper. Each per-depth stopper is logistic regression with scikit-learns default L2 regularisation on the eight features of Section 4.3, computed from readouts at their fitted temperatures. At depth one there is no earlier readout, so the features that compare with depth 1 take the values of an unchanged readout. The threshold is searched over 201 values in [0.5, 1]. The two folds of each panel are assigned by hash of the record group, so related questions share fold. Fitted on the calibration partition alone, the stopper has the threshold 0.915 for both Ouro models and 0.8075 for LEV-3B. Top-probability rule. question stops at the first depth whose top probability, after temperature scaling, reaches threshold. We choose this threshold on the calibration partition as the cheapest threshold whose accuracy is within one point of the deepest readout, which gives 0.81 for LEV-2.6B, 0.76 for LEV-1.4B, and 0.69 for LEV-3B. The label-free top-probability row sets one threshold the way the stoppers is set. Rules and variants. The margin and entropy rules choose their thresholds as the top-probability rule does. Patience-based exit stops once the answer has not changed for steps, so it needs at least three steps. The confidence features are the top probability, the margin, the normalised entropy, the log of the number of options, and the depth. The change features are the agreement with the previous answer, the KL divergence from the previous readout, the change of the top probability, and the depth. With two steps there is no earlier 24 answer at depth one, so the change features alone never stop LEV-3B. The correctness target predicts whether the answer at the current depth is right and is fitted on the labelled calibration partition, with its threshold chosen as for the top-probability rule. The label-free top-probability row keeps only the top probability as the stoppers feature, so its threshold on that score is set as the stoppers is, on unlabelled requests for 98% agreement with the deepest answer. Results. On the tuning panels, the top-probability rule of LEV-2.6B reaches 75.8% at cost of 0.69, 0.2 points below the frontier ([1.0, +0.6]). Against random escalation with the same distribution of stopping depths, the top-probability rule of LEV-2.6B gains 3.8 points on Kev-Seen ([+2.6, +5.0]), 2.5 on Kev-Transfer ([+1.0, +4.0]), and 2.2 on Kev-Skills ([+1.1, +3.3]).
